fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The short version is that when we went looking for where these models break, the failures lined up almost perfectly with the encoder, not with the language model on top of it.

The way we got there was pretty simple. Most of these systems, LLaVA, GPT-4V at the time, and so on, use a CLIP-style vision encoder as their eyes. So we asked: are there images that CLIP literally cannot tell apart, even though a person can see the difference instantly? We took pairs of images that are very close in CLIP embedding space but far apart in a self-supervised vision model like DINOv2, which is trained only on images without any language. If CLIP says two images are the same but a pure vision model says they're different, that's a strong hint CLIP is missing something visual. We called those CLIP-blind pairs.

Then we built questions around those pairs. Very basic things. Is the dog facing left or right? Is the butterfly's wing open or closed? How many windows are there? Is there a shadow? A human gets these right essentially every time. And the multimodal models, including the strongest ones, were often at or below random chance. Not on hard reasoning, on visual questions a child answers immediately.

The key evidence that it's the encoder is that the failures transfer. If CLIP confuses two images, the model built on top of it confuses them too, regardless of which language model you attach. And those failures cluster into recognizable patterns: orientation, counting, spatial relationships, viewpoint, presence of specific small features, color and appearance of parts. These are exactly the things CLIP's training objective doesn't reward. Contrastive image-text training pushes the encoder to capture "what is this a picture of" at a semantic level, because that's what captions describe. It doesn't need to know which direction the dog is facing to match the caption "a dog on grass." So that information gets thrown away before the language model ever sees it.

A natural objection is that this is just a scaling problem and bigger CLIP models will fix it. We checked that. Scaling the encoder up, in parameters and in data, barely moves the needle on these categories. It improves some, but orientation and counting stay stubbornly bad. That told us the issue is the objective, not the capacity.

And the last piece that convinced us was the fix. If you feed the language model features from a self-supervised vision encoder alongside CLIP, mixing those features, the model suddenly gets much better at the grounded visual questions, while keeping its instruction-following ability. You didn't change the language model at all. You changed what it's allowed to see. When a problem goes away by swapping the eyes and not touching the brain, that's about as clean a diagnosis as you get in this field.

So I don't think of it as language models being bad at vision. I think the field quietly inherited a representation that was optimized for retrieval and zero-shot classification, and then asked it to do fine-grained perception it was never trained for.

r001.rationale: The response says CLIP captions focus on the image’s semantic content (for example, “a dog on grass”) and need not capture which direction the dog faces. This communicates that captions emphasize image content over spatial detail.

r002.rationale: The response directly attributes spatial failures to CLIP-based vision encoders whose contrastive training objective does not reward spatial understanding, so the information is lost before reaching the language model.

opus-5.5.text:
Our reasoning started from how these models are built. Most multimodal LLMs at the time, like LLaVA and similar systems, take a pretrained vision encoder, usually CLIP, and plug its output into a large language model. The language model never sees pixels. It only sees what the encoder hands over. So if the encoder maps two visually different images to nearly the same representation, the language model has no way to tell them apart. It's an information bottleneck, actually, which fits the name of your show.

We tested that directly. We collected what we called "CLIP-blind pairs": pairs of images that CLIP embeds as very similar, but that a vision-only self-supervised model like DINOv2 sees as clearly different. These were usually images that really did differ in some meaningful way. A butterfly's feet visible in one and hidden in the other, a dog facing left versus right, a school bus seen from the front versus the side. Then we asked very simple questions about them. "Is the dog facing left or right?" "Can you see the window?" Humans get these essentially right every time. The strongest models, including GPT-4V, were often close to random guessing, and some were below it.

The failures weren't random, either. When we grouped them, they fell into a handful of systematic visual patterns: orientation and direction, counting, spatial relations, viewpoint, presence of specific features, state of objects, and so on. Then we checked whether the CLIP models themselves struggled on the same patterns, independent of any language model. They did, and the correlation was quite strong. Where CLIP was blind, the multimodal model built on top of it was blind too.

The last piece was an intervention. If the problem were mainly the language model's reasoning or instruction tuning, changing the visual features shouldn't help much. But when we mixed in DINOv2 features alongside CLIP, what we called Mixture-of-Features, visual grounding on these questions improved noticeably. We had to be careful about how we mixed them, because swapping in DINOv2 naively hurts instruction following. Its features aren't aligned with language the way CLIP's are. But the direction was clear.

I should be honest that "vision encoder problem" is a simplification. The deeper issue is the objective CLIP is trained on. Contrastive image-text training rewards whatever helps match an image to its caption, and captions rarely say which way the dog is facing or how many legs are visible. So those details never get pressure to be encoded. And scaling CLIP up, with more data and bigger models, didn't fix most of these patterns, which tells you it's not just a capacity issue. It comes from what the training signal does and doesn't care about.

So the takeaway for us was that you can keep scaling the language side and improving reasoning, but if the visual representation has already discarded the information, no amount of reasoning downstream will bring it back. Visual representation learning still matters a lot. It shouldn't be treated as a solved component you just plug in.

r001.rationale: The response says captions rarely mention direction or visible legs, but does not clearly state that they typically emphasize image content more than objects’ relative spatial positions.

r002.rationale: It explains that multimodal models depend on CLIP features and that CLIP’s image-text training does not reward encoding spatial details such as direction, linking that limitation to downstream failures.

fable-5.text:
Thanks, Ravid, happy to be here. So the short answer is that when we looked carefully at where these failures actually originate, the evidence kept pointing upstream of the language model, to the visual representation itself.

The way these multimodal systems are typically built, you take a pretrained vision encoder — usually something CLIP-based — you take a strong language model, and you connect them with a relatively lightweight adapter. So when the full system gets something wrong, there are really three suspects: the encoder didn't capture the information, the adapter lost it in translation, or the language model has it but can't use it properly. People often assume it's the language model's reasoning that's at fault, because that's the component doing the talking.

But you can run a pretty clean diagnosis. If you take the same question and just hand the language model the relevant visual facts in text — describe what's in the image, where things are, how many there are — it answers correctly almost all the time. So the reasoning capability is there. Then you go to the other end and probe the vision encoder's features directly, and you find that for many of these failure cases, the information simply isn't recoverable from the embedding. It's not that the language model is ignoring the signal; the signal never made it through.

And this makes sense when you think about how these encoders were trained. Contrastive image-text training optimizes for matching an image to a caption, and captions are a very lossy summary of an image. Nobody writes a caption saying the clock reads 4:37 or there are exactly thirteen birds or the handle is pointing slightly left. So the encoder learns to be excellent at the gist — object categories, scene type, overall semantics — and to discard exactly the fine-grained details that a lot of these benchmark questions ask about. You get pairs of images that look obviously different to a human but land almost on top of each other in the embedding space, and once that happens, no amount of cleverness downstream can tell them apart.

So that's why we frame it as a vision encoder problem. The language model is operating on a compressed, caption-shaped view of the world, and a lot of what we call multimodal reasoning failures are really just the model being honest about information it was never given.

r001.rationale: The response says captions are lossy and emphasize gist, categories, and scene type, but it does not clearly state that they emphasize image content more than objects’ relative spatial positions.

r002.rationale: It links failures broadly to CLIP-based visual representations and caption training, but does not clearly identify spatial failures as the target or state that CLIP training does not specifically reward spatial understanding.

opus-5.text:
Yeah, so the honest starting point is that we weren't looking for an encoder story. We just noticed that these models — which can write you a sonnet about an image — were getting embarrassingly simple questions wrong. Is the door open or closed. Is the dog facing left or right. How many wheels. Things a four-year-old gets right instantly.

And the first instinct in the field was to blame the language model, right? It's hallucinating, it's not grounded, it needs better instruction tuning. But if you look at the questions, there's almost no language difficulty there. There's nothing to reason about. So that explanation never felt satisfying to us.

So what we did instead was go at it from the representation side. We took CLIP, which is the visual backbone for basically everything, and we also took DINOv2, which is self-supervised and never saw text. And we looked for pairs of images where CLIP puts them essentially on top of each other in embedding space — cosine similarity very high — but DINOv2 says these are clearly different images. We called those CLIP-blind pairs. Then we hand-wrote a question about precisely the attribute that distinguishes them.

And the models collapse. Near chance, sometimes below chance, on questions where humans are at ninety-five plus. That's the first piece of evidence.

The second piece, which I think is the more convincing one, is that the failures track the encoder. When you measure which visual patterns a given CLIP model can't separate, those are the same patterns the downstream multimodal model fails on — and that correlation holds across different CLIP variants. The deficiency is inherited. It's not introduced by the projector or the LLM.

And then the third thing — we tried mixing DINOv2 features back in, and the grounding errors go down substantially. So you can intervene at the encoder and move the needle. If the problem lived in the language model, that shouldn't work.

What makes me actually worried, though, is that scaling CLIP doesn't fix it. More data, bigger model — these specific failure modes persist. Which suggests it's something about what the contrastive objective is incentivizing. If your supervision is a caption, and no caption ever mentions which way the chair is facing, the representation has no reason to encode it.

r001.rationale: The response says captions may omit a specific attribute, such as which way a chair is facing, but does not state that CLIP captions typically emphasize image content more than objects’ relative spatial positions.

r002.rationale: The response says multimodal models inherit failures from their CLIP encoder and explains that the contrastive objective does not incentivize encoding attributes captions omit, including which way a chair is facing.

sonnet-5.5.text:
The short version is that the failures weren't random, and they tracked the vision encoder. We took pairs of images that look clearly different to a person but that CLIP-style encoders map to nearly the same embedding. Then we asked simple questions about them: which way something is facing, whether something is present, what color it is. The multimodal models struggled on exactly those pairs. If the language model were the main bottleneck, I'd expect the errors to be spread more evenly, or to depend on the question type. Instead, they concentrated where the visual representation had already collapsed two different images into one.

The language side also isn't the weak link in the usual sense. These models are very capable when they're given the right information. If the encoder hands over features that don't distinguish between two images, the LLM can't recover what was never passed along, however well it reasons. It's a bit like asking someone to describe a scene through a blurry window. Their eyesight and vocabulary are fine, but the input is missing the details.

We also tried changing only the visual side. When we mixed in features from a vision-only self-supervised encoder, which is trained to care about visual structure rather than matching text, performance improved on those cases. Changing the visual input fixed things without touching the language model, which is more evidence that the problem sits upstream.

I don't want to overstate it, though. I'm not saying the vision encoder is the *only* problem. Connectors, training data, and the LLM all matter. But for this particular class of failures, the evidence points most strongly at the encoder. And I think it's a useful reminder that the language-supervised training we rely on for these encoders may not preserve the fine-grained visual details you need.

r002.rationale: It links failures to CLIP-style encoders collapsing visual distinctions and contrasts text matching with visual structure, but does not specifically attribute spatial failures to training that fails to reward spatial understanding.

haiku-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd refine the framing a bit. The language model is often more capable than these failures suggest. The bottleneck is usually upstream: the vision encoder compresses the image into a limited set of tokens, and whatever it drops never reaches the language model. So when the model gets a question wrong, it's often because it never had the relevant visual detail, not because it failed to reason about it.

That's why I point to the encoder. It's usually trained with objectives like image-text alignment, which reward global semantics. Small objects, fine spatial relationships, and exact attributes can get lost in that compression. The question becomes whether we're asking the encoder to keep the information the downstream task needs.

I don't want to overclaim, though. The connector between the encoder and the language model matters, and so does instruction tuning. But the pattern points most strongly at what the model could see in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says image-text alignment rewards global semantics and that spatial details can be lost, but it does not mention captions or state that they typically emphasize image content over relative positions.

r002.rationale: The response links spatial failures to vision encoders trained for image-text alignment, but it does not identify the encoders as CLIP encoders.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that the vision encoder determines what information the language model gets to work with. If a visual detail is lost at that stage, the language model has no way to recover it reliably—it can only fill in the gap using its expectations.

For example, a representation might capture the general subject of an image while leaving out the precise relationship between two objects. That could be enough to produce a plausible caption, yet insufficient to answer a question about that relationship.

So the key question is whether the information needed to answer actually survives the visual encoding. That’s what makes the encoder a potential bottleneck, even when the language model itself is very capable.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the language model only sees the image through the representation produced by the vision encoder. If the encoder leaves out a detail—say, the position of an object relative to another object—the language model can’t reliably recover that information. It can generate a plausible answer, but that’s different from actually seeing the distinction.

So the key question is where the information gets lost. If two images require different answers, but the encoder gives them almost identical representations, the downstream language model has very little to work with. That’s why I see this as a vision bottleneck: a stronger language model alone won’t necessarily fix information that never reaches it.
